home.faq.title: Questions and answers
home.faq.iolTypes.question: What types of intraocular lenses are there?
home.faq.iolTypes.answer: Monofocal, multifocal, and toric IOLs are selected for the clinical task and the patient's lifestyle.
home.faq.glasses.question: Do I need glasses after surgery?
home.faq.glasses.answer: It depends on the lens type and the initial condition of vision. Premium IOLs may reduce dependence on glasses.
home.faq.phaco.question: What is phacoemulsification?
home.faq.phaco.answer: Phacoemulsification is a modern method of cataract removal using ultrasound and subsequent implantation of an intraocular lens.
home.faq.rfa.question: What is Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA)?
home.faq.rfa.answer: It is a minimally invasive procedure for treating heart rhythm disorders through controlled impact on the arrhythmia focus.
home.faq.pacemaker.question: When do I need a pacemaker?
home.faq.pacemaker.answer: A pacemaker is used for rhythm disorders when the heart needs regular electrical support.
home.faq.recovery.question: How long is recovery after surgery?
home.faq.recovery.answer: Recovery time depends on the procedure and the patient's condition; the follow-up plan is defined by the physician.

ophthalmology.title: Ophthalmology
ophthalmology.lead: Advanced developments in ophthalmology that change standards of medical care and restore quality of life for patients.
ophthalmology.phaco.title: Cataract phacoemulsification
ophthalmology.phaco.text1: The gold standard of modern ophthalmic surgery. The method fragments the clouded lens using high-frequency ultrasonic oscillations through a micro-incision.
ophthalmology.phaco.text2: The procedure takes 5 to 10 minutes, is performed under local drop anesthesia, and requires no sutures, ensuring fast patient recovery.
ophthalmology.iol.title: New generation intraocular lenses
ophthalmology.iol.text1: We offer premium optical solutions for any vision correction task. Our lenses are made of biocompatible hydrophobic materials that imitate the natural properties of the human crystalline lens.
ophthalmology.iol.text2: Premium optics include harmful blue-light filtering, aspheric design for improved contrast, and multifocal technologies.
ophthalmology.followup.title: Postoperative care after phaco
ophthalmology.followup.text1: A multifocal lens is an artificial crystalline lens that allows clear vision at distance, intermediate range, and near without glasses.
ophthalmology.followup.text2: After surgery, many patients live without glasses for the first time in years, while the clinic receives a clear protocol for observation and recovery.
cardiology.title: Cardiology
cardiology.lead: Advanced technologies for diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases: navigation systems, electrophysiology solutions, and equipment for complex clinical tasks.
cardiology.rhythm.title: Types of heart rhythm disorders: from a minor irregularity to serious arrhythmia
cardiology.rhythm.text: Describes the main types of arrhythmias - extrasystole, tachycardia, bradycardia, and atrial fibrillation - in simple language without complex terms.
cardiology.treatment.title: Arrhythmia treatment methods: when medication is enough and when surgery is needed
cardiology.treatment.text: Explains when tablets are sufficient and when interventional treatment is required, such as ablation or pacemaker implantation, and why surgery may be better.
cardiology.rfa.title: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA): how to seal the heart area causing arrhythmia
cardiology.rfa.text: A simple explanation of the RFA procedure: catheter -> heating the area -> eliminating arrhythmia, without pain and with fast recovery.
article.phaco.title: Cataract phacoemulsification
article.phaco.intro1: The gold standard of modern ophthalmic surgery. The method fragments the clouded lens using high-frequency ultrasonic oscillations through a micro-incision. After removal of the damaged lens masses, an intraocular lens is implanted to fully restore vision.
article.phaco.intro2: The procedure takes 5 to 10 minutes, is performed under local drop anesthesia, and requires no sutures, ensuring fast patient recovery.
article.phaco.what.title: What is phacoemulsification
article.phaco.what.subtitle: Operation principle:
article.phaco.what.step1: A phaco needle is inserted through a microscopic 2-3 mm puncture.
article.phaco.what.step2: The needle generates high-frequency oscillations, breaking the lens into small fragments.
article.phaco.what.step3: The fragmented masses are removed by an aspiration system through the same micro-incision.
article.phaco.what.step4: An artificial lens is implanted into the freed space and fixed in the capsular bag.
article.phaco.what.note: The operation lasts 10-20 minutes under local anesthesia without general anesthesia.
article.phaco.standard.title: Why phaco is the modern standard
article.phaco.standard.subtitle: Phaco combines key advantages:
article.phaco.standard.minimal: Minimally invasive: 2-3 mm puncture, no suturing required, and the wound closes quickly.
article.phaco.standard.painless: Painless: local anesthesia, so the patient does not feel discomfort.
article.phaco.standard.precision: High precision: optical biometry and 3D mapping help position the IOL accurately.
article.phaco.standard.lowRisk: Low risk of complications: minimal tissue damage reduces inflammation and edema.
article.phaco.standard.universal: Universal: the method is suitable for all cataract stages, including dense and complex cases.
article.phaco.standard.note: These facts are confirmed by clinical protocols of the Russian Ministry of Health and international ophthalmology associations.
article.phaco.stages.title: Operation stages
article.rhythm.title: What types of heart rhythm disorders occur
article.rhythm.intro1: Arrhythmia is a condition in which the heart beats too fast, too slowly, or irregularly. Some rhythm disorders feel like a brief irregular beat, while others require in-depth diagnostics and specialist observation.
article.rhythm.intro2: This material helps explain basic terms and why modern diagnostic and treatment methods are selected individually for the clinical task.
article.rhythm.types.title: Main types of disorders
article.rhythm.types.subtitle: The following are most often discussed in clinical practice:
article.rhythm.types.extrasystole: Extrasystole: premature contractions that the patient may feel as a skipped or irregular beat.
article.rhythm.types.tachycardia: Tachycardia: an accelerated rhythm that occurs in episodes or persists for a long time.
article.rhythm.types.bradycardia: Bradycardia: a slow rhythm assessed together with symptoms and the patient's condition.
article.rhythm.types.afib: Atrial fibrillation: an irregular rhythm that requires careful diagnostics and risk control.
article.rhythm.diagnostics.title: How rhythm is assessed
article.rhythm.diagnostics.text: Initial assessment uses ECG, 24-hour monitoring, and symptom data: attack frequency, physical load, comorbidities, and medications. The final approach depends on the cause of the disorder, its frequency, and its impact on quality of life.
article.rhythm.diagnostics.step1: Record complaints and the circumstances when irregular beats appear.
article.rhythm.diagnostics.step3: Assess risks and the need for further observation.
article.rhythm.diagnostics.step4: Select medication or interventional tactics if indicated.
article.rhythm.treatment.title: Modern treatment approaches
article.rhythm.treatment.text: In some cases, observation and correction of risk factors are enough; in others, medication therapy, catheter technologies, or implantable devices are used. The physician makes the decision after diagnostics and assessment of the patient's condition.
article.rhythm.note: This information is for reference and does not replace a physician consultation.
